ann_85.original: Direct plan and usage terms. A linear term in the log-odds (the formula is attached as evidence). Per sd of each z-scored input: voice-mail plan -1.00, evening minutes 0.81, international plan 0.72, day minutes 0.70, voicemail messages 0.40, night charge 0.26, international calls -0.20; the other terms are smaller. So the model gives international-plan holders a higher risk and voice-mail-plan holders a lower one, and more evening and day use raises risk. Self-probe on a typical customer: adding an international plan moves risk from 2% to 17%; a voice-mail plan with no messages gives below 1%, and with 25 messages below 1%. On the training data the 380 international-plan holders churn at 42.4% (mean predicted risk 43%), and the 1061 voice-mail-plan holders at 7.4%. For low spenders the day and evening terms are largely offset by the low-spend hinge. It is the most important leaf: switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.771.
ann_85.proposed: This part is a plain weighted sum: an international plan raises the predicted chance, more evening and daytime minutes raise it steadily, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.

ann_86.original: Direct state offsets. A fixed log-odds offset per state from the state indicators' own edges (formula attached as evidence). In a sweep of the state codes on a typical customer, this part gives Vermont -1.48, Alaska -0.93, Pennsylvania -0.68, California 1.25 and Washington 1.27, against -0.02 for Texas, which has no edge. Self-probe: the predicted risk of the typical customer is 1% in Vermont and 7% in California, against 2% in Texas. These offsets rest on small state samples: California's is fitted to 41 rows (churn 26.8%, mean predicted risk 27%) and Vermont's to 80 rows (churn 6.2%, mean predicted risk 7%). Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.900.
ann_86.proposed: This part adds a fixed amount for each of a set of states, raising the predicted chance in Washington and California and lowering it in Vermont and Alaska.

ann_87.original: State gate units. Five hidden units that each read one to three state indicators. The Missouri unit is the one that matters: in a state sweep on a typical customer, this part gives Missouri -1.82 in the log-odds against -0.22 for Texas, which no gate reads. The other gated states move less: West Virginia -0.48, Indiana -0.39, Washington -0.42, Wisconsin 0.03, South Carolina -0.17; Oregon, which enters the Indiana/Washington unit negatively, gets -0.22, as Texas. Self-probe: the typical customer's predicted risk is below 1% in Missouri against 2% in Texas. The Missouri effect is fitted to 80 rows; those customers churn at 11.2% while the model gives them 7% on average, so the offset is stronger than the data alone suggests. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.908.
ann_87.proposed: This part adds further state shifts through small switches, mainly lowering the predicted chance in Missouri.

ann_88.original: Heavy daytime use. This hinge reads total day minutes (plus a small New York term) and adds risk for heavy daytime users; below a threshold it is off. Holding a typical customer and sweeping day minutes, the unit is off at 211 minutes (0.000) and on at 212 (0.006). It is on for 1124 of the 4000 training customers; no customer under 211 day minutes has it on (0 rows), and of the 1113 customers with 212 or more day minutes it is off for 2, both in New York (2 rows with state New York in that group), whose indicator raises the threshold slightly. Through this part, the customers it acts on get 1.22 added to the log-odds on average; their churn rate is 25.7% against 9.6% for the rest. The unit feeds the score with weight 2.24, on top of the direct day-minutes edge of 0.70 per sd, so above the threshold risk rises much faster with day minutes than below it. In the whole model, a typical customer with 180 day minutes ($30.6) has predicted risk 2% and one with 260 minutes ($44.2) 22%. Switching this part off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.880.
ann_88.proposed: This switch adds to the predicted chance for heavy daytime users: nothing until about 212 minutes of daytime use, then steadily.

ann_89.original: Low-spend floor. This hinge is on for customers whose day and evening charges are low (it falls with both charges and rises with customer-service calls; Connecticut and New Hampshire indicators also raise it). It does not mark a high-churn group: the 2231 customers it acts on churn at 10.6%, against 18.6% for the rest. Instead it offsets the direct usage terms, which give these customers -0.74 on average, while this part adds 1.17 for them (log-odds). The effect is that predicted risk stops falling with lower use and rises again at very low use. Self-probe, typical customer with day minutes and day charge moved together: at 100 minutes ($17) risk is 2%, higher than 2% at 180 minutes ($30.6); without this part the 100-minute case would be 1%. The unit value is 2.45 at a $20 day charge and $12 evening charge and 0.00 at $40 and $22. It also makes service calls count for low spenders: for the typical customer this part adds 0.03 at one call and 0.83 at four. Its weight into the score is 0.91. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.884.
ann_89.proposed: This floor adds to the predicted chance for customers with low daytime and evening charges, and a higher charge of either kind lowers it in an uneven way.

ann_90.original: Service calls without heavy day spending. A chain that opens when a customer makes many customer-service calls and has a low or moderate day charge; it then adds a large amount of risk. The day charge closes the gate through a middle unit; a unit reading international minutes and a Tennessee indicator damps that middle unit, so fewer international minutes (or a Tennessee address) let the gate stay open at a higher day charge. A second unit amplifies the gate's output (weights 1.63 and 1.61 into the score). Self-probe, typical customer (day charge about $31): the gate is shut at three calls (unit value 0.00, risk 3%) and open at four (0.15, risk 5%); risk is 43% at five calls and 91% at six. With five calls, the part adds 3.45 to the log-odds at a $30 day charge and 0.00 at $35 (risk 63% against 3%). International minutes are a partner: with five calls and a $30 day charge, risk is 90% at 5 international minutes and 21% at 15. On the training data no customer with fewer than three calls has the gate open (0 rows). Of the 318 customers with four or more calls, who churn at 50.0%, the gate is open for 180; the 138 with the gate shut churn at 23.2%. It also opens for 221 customers with exactly three calls and a very low day charge; they churn at 5.9% while the model gives them 13% on average, so the gate's reach to three calls is not supported by the data. Across the 401 customers it acts on it adds 2.14 to the log-odds on average. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.848.
ann_90.proposed: This gate adds to the predicted chance for customers who call customer service more often and do not have a high daytime charge, rising slowly at first, then faster with the calls.

ann_91.original: International minutes. A hinge that adds risk once international minutes pass roughly the typical level and grows with them. Self-probe on a typical customer: the unit is off at 8 minutes (0.00) and on at 10 (0.28); risk goes from 1% at 8 minutes to 4% at 16. It acts on 2651 customers, adding 0.39 to their log-odds on average (weight 0.40); they churn at 15.0% against 12.5%. International minutes also act in the other direction inside the service-call gate (more minutes keep that gate shut), so their whole-model effect depends on service calls. Switching this part off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.905.
ann_91.proposed: This switch adds to the predicted chance once international minutes pass about 9 minutes, then steadily.

ann_92.original: Long-standing accounts. A hinge that adds a small amount of risk for accounts older than a threshold between 140 and 150 days, on top of a small direct account-length edge. Self-probe on a typical customer: the unit is off at 140 days (0.00) and on at 150 (0.07); risk goes from 2% at 100 days to 3% at 200, of which this part gives 0.32 in log-odds at 200 days. It acts on 469 customers, adding 0.13 on average; they churn at 15.8% against 13.9%. It matters little: switching it off changes the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.908.
ann_92.proposed: This switch adds a very small amount once the account length passes about 147, then steadily.

ann_93.original: Voicemail messages. A hinge that adds a very small amount of risk per voicemail message once a customer has more than a few messages. Self-probe, typical customer with a voice-mail plan: the unit is off at 0 messages (0.00) and on at 10 (0.04); at 50 messages it adds 0.13 to the log-odds. It acts on 1054 customers, adding 0.06 on average (weight 0.05). The larger message effect is the direct edge (0.40 per sd, in the direct usage terms). Switching this part off changes the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.908: it is close to inert.
ann_93.proposed: This switch adds a very small amount once the number of voice-mail messages passes about 10 messages, then steadily.

ann_94.original: State effects. Each state's total offset is its direct edge plus the state-gate units, added in the log-odds. For a typical customer otherwise unchanged, predicted risk is below 1% in Missouri, 1% in Vermont, 2% in Texas (no state term), 6% in Washington and 7% in California. Switching the whole group off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.900.
ann_94.proposed: This part gives each state its own fixed shift in the predicted chance, from below 1% in Missouri to about 7% in California for a typical customer.

ann_95.original: Day usage and service calls. The heavy-day-use hinge, the low-spend floor and the service-call gate add in the log-odds. Together they make predicted risk U-shaped in day usage and make customer-service calls matter for customers who are not heavy daytime spenders. Self-probe, typical customer with day minutes and charge moved together. With one service call, risk is 2% at 100 minutes ($17), 2% at 180 minutes ($30.6) and 22% at 260 minutes ($44.2). With five calls it is 94%, 45% and 22% at the same three usage levels: service calls raise risk sharply for low and typical users, while for the heavy user both call-reading parts are off and the calls leave the prediction where it was. This is the most important group: switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.757.
ann_95.proposed: Heavy daytime use raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, adding nothing until about 212 minutes of daytime use, then steadily. Calls to customer service raise it, slowly at first, then faster, mainly when total daytime charge is at or below 30.69 US dollars.

ann_96.original: Minor usage hinges. Three single-input hinges (international minutes, account length, voicemail messages), added in the log-odds; each adds risk above its own threshold. International minutes carry most of the group's weight. Switching the whole group off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.904, against 0.905 for the international-minutes hinge alone.
ann_96.proposed: This part adds three small switches, for international minutes, account length and voice-mail messages, each adding to the predicted chance past its own point.

ann_97.original: Churn score. The predicted churn probability is the sigmoid of the output bias plus the four groups added in the log-odds: the direct plan and usage terms, the state effects, the day-usage and service-call group, and the minor usage hinges. On the 4000 training customers the mean predicted risk is 14% against a churn rate of 14.1%, and the training AUC is 0.908. The model's main churn signals are an international plan, many service calls by customers who are not heavy daytime spenders, and heavy daytime use; a voice-mail plan lowers risk. Self-probe: the typical customer has risk 2%; with five service calls 43%; with an international plan 17%; with both 90%. The two effects add in the log-odds (scores -4.06, -0.30, -1.59, 2.17), because the plan acts through its own edge and the calls through hidden parts. By AUC loss when switched off, the largest parts are the day-usage and service-call group (0.757), the direct plan and usage terms (0.771) and the service-call gate (0.848).
ann_97.proposed: The model adds four parts together into one score for the chance that a customer leaves. An international plan raises the predicted chance from about 2% to about 17% for a typical customer, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to below 1% (with the voice-mail messages such customers typically have).

parts.name: churn_score
parts.original_hypothesis: Churn score. The predicted churn probability is the sigmoid of the output bias plus the four groups added in the log-odds: the direct plan and usage terms, the state effects, the day-usage and service-call group, and the minor usage hinges. On the 4000 training customers the mean predicted risk is 14% against a churn rate of 14.1%, and the training AUC is 0.908. The model's main churn signals are an international plan, many service calls by customers who are not heavy daytime spenders, and heavy daytime use; a voice-mail plan lowers risk. Self-probe: the typical customer has risk 2%; with five service calls 43%; with an international plan 17%; with both 90%. The two effects add in the log-odds (scores -4.06, -0.30, -1.59, 2.17), because the plan acts through its own edge and the calls through hidden parts. By AUC loss when switched off, the largest parts are the day-usage and service-call group (0.757), the direct plan and usage terms (0.771) and the service-call gate (0.848).
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: day_use_and_service_calls
parts.original_hypothesis: Day usage and service calls. The heavy-day-use hinge, the low-spend floor and the service-call gate add in the log-odds. Together they make predicted risk U-shaped in day usage and make customer-service calls matter for customers who are not heavy daytime spenders. Self-probe, typical customer with day minutes and charge moved together. With one service call, risk is 2% at 100 minutes ($17), 2% at 180 minutes ($30.6) and 22% at 260 minutes ($44.2). With five calls it is 94%, 45% and 22% at the same three usage levels: service calls raise risk sharply for low and typical users, while for the heavy user both call-reading parts are off and the calls leave the prediction where it was. This is the most important group: switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.757.
variables: number of calls to customer service
